prompt: Which fiber types carry DCML information from the periphery?
explain: DCML information travels on large, heavily myelinated fibers: A-alpha (Ia/Ib, from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs) and A-beta (type II and cutaneous mechanoreceptor afferents). Their fast conduction suits precise, rapid proprioception and fine touch. A-alpha (Ia/Ib) and A-beta (type II) fibers.

prompt: Name the cutaneous receptors served by the DCML pathway.
answer: Meissner, Merkel, Pacinian and Ruffini endings
explain: DCML serves the encapsulated or specialised mechanoreceptors of the skin (Meissner for light touch, Merkel for pressure and texture, Pacinian for vibration, Ruffini for stretch), plus muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs for conscious proprioception. Plus muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs for proprioception.

prompt: A lesion of the right dorsal column in the lumbar spinal cord causes loss of vibration sense on which side?
explain: DCML first-order axons ascend uncrossed in the dorsal column and only decussate in the caudal medulla (internal arcuate fibers). A lumbar dorsal column lesion therefore removes vibration sense on the same (right) side as the lesion. Ipsilateral: the axons have not yet crossed.

prompt: A lesion of the left medial lemniscus in the pons causes loss of fine touch on which side of the body?
explain: After the internal arcuate fibers cross in the caudal medulla, the medial lemniscus carries information from the opposite side of the body. A left pontine medial lemniscus lesion therefore causes loss of fine touch on the right side. Contralateral: the axons crossed in the caudal medulla.

source.ref: lecture-5, lecture-9, Sensory Pathway Cheat Sheet, lab-5

prompt: How many neurons carry DCML information from receptor to cortex, and where is the last cell body?
explain: The DCML relay has three neurons: the first-order cell body is in the dorsal root ganglion, the second-order in the gracile or cuneate nucleus (axons cross as internal arcuate fibers), and the third-order in the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, which projects to cortex. DRG, gracile/cuneate nucleus, then VPL thalamus.

prompt: Which two fiber types carry pain/temperature information into the cord?
explain: Pain and temperature enter on A-delta fibers (thin, lightly myelinated, fast) and C fibers (unmyelinated, slow). Thin fibers have slower conduction than the A-alpha/A-beta fibers of the dorsal column system. A-delta are lightly myelinated; C fibers are unmyelinated.

prompt: Which fiber type carries fast, sharp, well-localised pain?
explain: A-delta fibers are lightly myelinated, so they conduct faster than C fibers and carry the first, sharp, well-localised pain. C fibers carry the later, dull pain.

source.ref: lecture-5, lecture-9, Sensory Pathway Cheat Sheet, lab-5

prompt: Which fiber type carries slow, dull, burning pain?
explain: C fibers are unmyelinated and conduct slowly, so they carry the delayed, dull, burning, poorly localised second pain, following the sharp first pain of A-delta fibers.

Contralateral: second-order axons have already crossed.

prompt: In the sympathetic system, are the preganglionic and postganglionic fibers short or long?

prompt: What do alpha versus gamma motor neurons innervate?
answer: Alpha: extrafusal fibers; gamma: intrafusal fibers
explain: Alpha motor neurons innervate extrafusal fibers, which generate force. Gamma motor neurons innervate the intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindle, keeping the spindle taut so it stays sensitive to stretch as the muscle contracts.

Gamma: intrafusal fibers: intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindle
